newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco settlement would prompt spin-offs-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco settlement would prompt spin-offs-analysts.

text.p: RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp would likely move quickly to divest its food unit if the tobacco industry settles its lawsuits, but the picture is less clear for other cigarette makers.

Mired in a mountain of litigation, the tobacco industry is holding talks with state officials over a possible settlement of lawsuits. However, the talks are not expected to result in any deal for months as both sides wrestle over a host of issues, including a proposed $300 billion to be paid by the industry into a fund for smoking-related injuries.
Investors and analysts have long contended that non-tobacco businesses held by cigarette companies are undervalued and burdened by their affiliation with the controversial industry.

In any of the cases, industry experts said the potential of a spin-off would depend greatly on the breadth of a potential settlement, explaining that tobacco companies would only spin off units if guaranteed they would be protected against any future lawsuits.

"If reached, a comprehensive settlement...could lead to a separation of the tobacco and non-tobacco operations of both Philip Morris and RJR Nabisco," wrote Thomas Hoens, tobacco analyst at Fitch Investors Service Inc in a recent report.
RJR, which has been under intense pressure to spin off its 80.5 percent-owned Nabisco Holdings Corp unit, has repeatedly said it would do so if the cloud of litigation diminished.
"It would do it the next day" if a broad settlement was signed, said David Adelman of Dean Witter.
The maker of Camel cigarettes and Oreo cookies has never set a date for a spin-off, saying only that it would break apart the businesses at an appropriate time.
"I can't think of a more appropriate time than reaching a comprehensive settlement" of tobacco litigation, Hoens said.

Of all tobacco companies, RJR is viewed as benefiting most from a spin-off of its food business. Most shareholders have supported the company's decision to wait, crushing a proxy battle last year waged by investors Carl Icahn and Bennett LeBow, who contended an immediate spin-off would significantly raise the company's stock price.
A spokeswoman for RJR declined to discuss the implications that a settlement would have for a Nabisco spin-off. The company also has repeatedly declined to discuss the settlement talks.

Industry experts said both of RJR's businesses were well positioned to operate on their own, speculating that a spin-off would be structured so that the tobacco unit would carry most of the debt load to enable the food company to operate on more equal footing with its peers.
Although a spin-off is likely in RJR's future, the issue is less certain for Philip Morris Cos Inc, maker of Marlboro cigarettes and Oscar Mayer hot dogs.
Philip Morris has considered a spin-off in the past but opted against such a move, and it is not facing pressure from shareholders to break apart its two flourishing businesses.
"I could see them revisiting the question," Hoens said.
A Philip Morris spokesman declined to comment.

Although crediting Philip Morris management for strong performance in both businesses, "there's not a lot of synergy there," said Don Yacktman, whose Yacktman Asset Management Co holds more than two million shares.

Industry experts gave less likelihood to a spin-off by Loews Corp, whose Lorillard unit makes Newport cigarettes and other brands. They said the company, which also owns hotels and most of insurance company CNA Financial Corp, typically uses cash flow from its thriving businesses to invest in its others.
A spokeswoman for Loews could not be reached for comment.
